podcast.body: Johnny Ramone, the guitarist for the Ramones, lost his battle with prostate cancer in September 2004, becoming the third original member of the band to pass away. "Whereas Johnny Ramon lost his fight with prostate cancer in September 2004..."

podcast.title: Founding Member of The Ramones
podcast.body: In 1973, John Cummings (who later became Johnny Ramone) visited Manie's Music with Douglas Colvin to purchase instruments after deciding to form a band. A year later, they formed The Ramones with Joey and Tommy, with their initial instrument purchases being a guitar, a bass, and a small amp from the store. "A year later, Douglas was calling himself D.D. and Johnny was Johnny. And together with Joey and Tommy, they formed the Ramones."

xref.title: Backstage Window Encounter (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash recounted how he, Johnny Rotten, and members of the Sex Pistols met The Ramones backstage at the Roundhouse by throwing a rock at a window. Johnny Ramone stuck his head out, and the British punks introduced themselves, being subsequently pulled up through the window in a "human chain" to get in. "And so they kind of formed a sort of human chain and pulled us up through this window. And that was the first time we met him and that was just a really great punk rock moment."

xref.title: Fractured Skull Attack (August 1983) – Street Brawl Led to Brain Surgery, Later Distrust of Doctors, and Death
xref.body: In August 1983, Johnny Ramone became involved in a brawl with Seth Maclin of a band called Sub Zero Construction on the street outside Johnny's East Village apartment at 4am. Johnny was beaten to the pavement and kicked in the head. He was rushed to hospital with a fractured skull and required brain surgery. He recovered, but the incident left him deeply distrustful of doctors. When he later began experiencing abdominal pain — roughly 15 years after the attack — his mistrust caused him to delay seeking treatment. The abdominal pain was aggressive prostate cancer that spread throughout his body. Chemotherapy failed, and Johnny died on September 15, 2004. "Had he not been beaten up in the summer of 1983 and still trusted doctors?"

xref.title: Final Show and Legacy (1996)
xref.body: After their appearance at Lollapalooza in the summer of 1996, The Ramones played their last show in Hollywood, concluding a career that spanned 2,263 performances and finally receiving deserved recognition for their contributions before the deaths of Joey and Johnny Ramone. "After that summer, they would play their last show in Hollywood, bringing the curtain down on a career that included 2,263 shows."

xref.title: Deaths of Original Members (2001-2014)
xref.body: The original lineup of the Ramones tragically passed away over a 13-year period: Joey Ramone in 2001, Dee Dee Ramone in 2002, Johnny Ramone in 2004, and Tommy Ramone in 2014, marking the end of an era for the seminal punk band. "He was the first of the original Ramones to die. Base player DD Ramon died of a heroin overdose the following summer. Whereas Johnny Ramon lost his fight with prostate cancer in September 2004, and drummer Tommy Ramon was taken by Bile Duck Cancer in the summer of 2014."

xref.title: Band Formation Idea
xref.body: D.D. Ramone and Johnny Ramone conceived the idea to form a band after smoking weed together following work, leading to their trip to Mani's Music. "It was him and Johnny who got the idea to form a band in the first place after smoking weed after work."

xref.title: Contribution to the Formation of The Ramones
xref.body: Henry Goldrich indirectly played a role in the formation of The Ramones. In 1973, Douglas Colvin and John Cummings visited Manie's Music after deciding to form a band while high. They purchased a guitar, a bass, and a small amp from the store, which were the foundational instruments for the band they would form a year later, as D.D. and Johnny Ramone with Joey and Tommy Ramone. "The Ramones, another band made possible by Henry Goldrich, the proprietor of Manie's music in New York."

xref.title: Death Date Coincidence – 37 Years After Ian Curtis, Close to Chester Bennington
xref.body: Cornell died by hanging on May 18, 2017 — exactly 37 years to the day that Joy Division singer Ian Curtis hanged himself. Two months later, on July 20, 2017 (which would have been Cornell's 53rd birthday), his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide, also by hanging. Cornell is interred at Hollywood Forever Cemetery in Los Angeles; his tombstone reads "Voice of our generation and an artist for all time." Johnny Ramone's monument is nearby. "Two months after Chris died, July 20, 2017, which would have been Chris' 53rd birthday, his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Enduring Animosity
xref.body: Despite Johnny Ramone and Linda Danielle marrying in 1984, The Ramones remained together and continued touring until 1996. Joey Ramone did not speak to Linda again until 1993, and he and Johnny almost never spoke again until the band's breakup. The feud was intense and quiet, prioritizing the band's business over personal issues. Johnny did not contact Joey when he was dying in early 2000 nor attend his funeral. "Joey didn't speak to Linda again until 1993. And Joey and Johnny almost never spoke again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fifteen-Year Feud Between Joey and Johnny
xref.body: Joey Ramone and Johnny Ramone, despite being in the same band and sharing all aspects of their professional lives, did not speak to each other for 15 years. This was largely due to Joey's girlfriend, Linda, leaving him for Johnny, whom she later married. Their political differences (Joey liberal, Johnny Republican) also contributed to the tension. "Joey's girlfriend Linda left him for Johnny whom she later married. The tension and the jealousy was unbelievable and it lasted more than 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Lineup Change – Drummer to Frontman
xref.body: The Ramones were formed in early 1974, with Jeff Hyman (later Joey Ramone) on drums, John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) on guitar, and Douglas Colvin (later D.D. Ramone) on bass. Their first gig was on March 30, 1974. Due to Jeff's powerful, fast drumming style and his superior singing ability, he transitioned to lead vocalist, with a friend named Tommy taking over on drums using a basic $100 kit. "This arrangements worked out pretty good Especially after John became Johnny and Douglas became D.D. and Jeff adopted the name Joey and they all adopted the same last name Ramon."

xref.title: Heartbreak Over Linda and Johnny Ramone (Unspecified Period)
xref.body: Joey Ramone experienced severe heartbreak when Linda, whom he believed was "the one," left him for his bandmate Johnny Ramone and subsequently married Johnny. This event led to a lasting estrangement, with Joey reportedly never forgiving either of them and ceasing to speak with Johnny for over a decade despite their continued band membership. "He really thought Linda was the one. But then she left him for bandmate Johnny Ramon and would later marry him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Decades-Long Feud (Post-Linda Breakup)
xref.body: Joey Ramone was deeply heartbroken when his girlfriend Linda left him for his bandmate Johnny Ramone, whom she later married. Joey never forgave either of them, and despite remaining in the same band until the end, Joey and Johnny reportedly never spoke to each other after Linda changed relationships, leading to a decade of silence between them during band activities. "The story is that although they were in the same band together to the end, Joey and Johnny never spoke a word to each other after Linda changed teams."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Long-Standing Feud
xref.body: For much of the Ramones' existence until their official end in August 1996, Joey Ramone and Johnny Ramone did not speak to each other due to Joey's girlfriend, Linda, breaking up with him and subsequently marrying Johnny. "And for much of that time, they never spoke, because Joey's girlfriend Linda broke up with him and started dating Johnny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey's Girlfriend Incident
xref.body: Despite not being biological brothers, Joey and Johnny Ramone had a severe falling out that lasted for years after Johnny became romantically involved with and subsequently married Joey's girlfriend. "Joey and Johnny Ramone didn't talk to each other for years after Johnny stole and then married Joey's girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone and The Beatles
xref.body: An anecdote recounts Johnny Ramone attending The Beatles' concert at Shea Stadium on August 23, 1966, armed with a bag of rocks, which he then threw at the band. "there's another story that says that when the Beatles played Shay Stadium in August 23, 1966, Johnny went to the show with a big bag of rocks, which she then proceeded to throw at the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone – Documented All 2,262 Ramones Gigs
xref.body: As the Ramones' de facto leader, chief strategist, and disciplinarian, Johnny Ramone made most business decisions, dictated what everyone wore on stage, controlled practice schedules, approved every set list, and scrupulously documented every single one of the 2,262 gigs the Ramones ever played. "Johnny was the one who scrupulously documented every single one of the 2,262 gigs the Ramones ever played."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's "Straight-Edge" Lifestyle
xref.body: Johnny Ramone ceased drug use in his early 20s, abstained from alcohol, and approached his work with the Ramones in a highly regimented, disciplined, and job-like manner. "Johnny stopped doing drugs when he was in his early 20s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Alternative Healing Attempt
xref.body: In an attempt to combat his cancer, Johnny Ramone underwent a few rounds of treatment with a "new age healer" from Vancouver, but these efforts proved unsuccessful. "There were also a few rounds with a new age healer from Vancouver, but that didn't work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Cancer Progression and Pain
xref.body: After numerous rounds of chemotherapy that caused him to go bald and feel self-conscious, scans in 2003 revealed his cancer had metastasized to his bones, lung, and bladder, leading to dangerously low blood counts and tremendous pain, which he disliked treating with painkillers. "In 2003, scans showed that the cancer had spread to his bones, his lung, and his bladder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Catholic Upbringing Trauma
xref.body: Johnny Ramone harbored strong negative feelings against his Catholic upbringing, claiming that he had been physically abused by nuns. "He also harbored strong feelings against his Catholic upbringing, saying that he was physically abused by nuns."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Cenotaph at Hollywood Forever Cemetery
xref.body: Although his ashes are held by his wife Linda, a notable cenotaph dedicated to Johnny Ramone is located at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery, situated not far from D.D. Ramone's burial site. "Linda has his ashes, but there is a fantastic cenotaph at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Conservative Politics
xref.body: Johnny Ramone was known as a hardcore Republican, one of the most conservative punk rockers. He openly admired and worshipped Ronald Reagan. This political stance often put him at odds with Joey Ramone, especially when he had to perform anti-Reagan songs written by Joey, such as "Bonzo Goes to Bitburg."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Death
xref.body: Johnny Ramone passed away on September 15, 2004, at his home in Los Angeles, after a long battle with aggressive prostate cancer. "Johnny hung on until September 15, 2004, when he died at his home in LA."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Death and Memorial
xref.body: Johnny Ramone died on October 8, 2004, at the age of 55, after a five-year battle with prostate cancer. He was cremated, but an eight-foot bronze statue of him stands in Hollywood Forever Cemetery, not far from Dee Dee's grave. "He died on October 8, 2004, after suffering from prostate cancer for five years. He was 55."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Discipline and Baseball Fandom
xref.body: Johnny Cummings (Johnny Ramone) came from a blue-collar background and attended military schools, instilling in him a strong sense of discipline. He was a lifelong, fervent fan of the New York Yankees, with stories of him having a TV set up just off stage to watch games while performing gigs. "His parents hoped that he turned out to be a pro baseball player. And there were stories about how when there was a big game on, Johnny would have a TV set up just off stage so he could play the gig and watch the game at the same time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Friendship with Kurt Hammett
xref.body: Johnny Ramone was frequently visited by Kurt Hammett of Metallica, who shared a significant interest in horror movie posters with him. "He was often visited by Kurt Hammett of Metallica, who also had a major thing for horror movie posters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Love for Baseball and Disney
xref.body: Johnny Ramone's greatest pleasure was baseball, which explains the baseball bat prominently featured in the Ramones' logo, and he also collected cards and memorabilia related to the sport. He also enjoyed visiting Disney World and Disneyland and collected movie posters. "His greatest pleasure was baseball. And that explains the baseball bat and the Ramones logo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Personal Collections
xref.body: Inside his Hollywood Hills home, Johnny Ramone kept his extensive baseball collection, Disney memorabilia, movie posters, a room dedicated to Elvis, and various stuffed animals, including a two-headed calf. "Inside was his baseball collection, his Disney memorabilia, his movie posters, a room dedicated to Elvis, and a bunch of stuffed game, including a two-headed calf."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Pink Hollywood Hills Ranch House
xref.body: At the time of his illness, Johnny Ramone resided in a pink-painted, gated ranch house in the Hollywood Hills, partially financed by the sale of some of his renowned guitars, one of which fetched $937,000. "By this time, he was living in a gated ranch house up on the Hollywood hills that was painted pink, something that was partly financed by selling some of his famous guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Political Views
xref.body: Johnny Ramone was a staunch political conservative, an unusual stance for a punk musician, openly supporting Ronald Reagan, both Bushes, and identifying as a major Republican. "Johnny was a hardcore political conservative. He loved Ronald Reagan and both Bushes and was a major Republican supporter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Post-Mortem Sentiments
xref.body: Johnny Ramone expressed his lack of desire to interact with Joey Ramone even in death, stating he wouldn't want Joey at his funeral and wouldn't want to hear from him if he were dying, preferring to be left alone by friends. "I was in California, said Johnny. I wasn't going to travel all the way to New York, but I wouldn't have gone anyway. I wouldn't want him coming to my funeral and I wouldn't want to hear from him if I were dying."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
xref.body: In 1999, at age 51, despite his health-conscious "straight-edge punk" lifestyle, Johnny Ramone was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer, which ranked as a nine on an oncology scale of ten. "In 1999 at the age of 51, and despite being a health-conscious straight-edge punk, Johnny was diagnosed with prostate cancer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Reaction to Joey's Illness and Death
xref.body: Johnny Ramone reportedly refused to visit or call Joey while he was dying in the hospital and did not attend his funeral, reflecting the deep personal tensions between them. "There were stories that when Joey lay dying in the hospital, Johnny refused to visit or call."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kurt Hammett's Friendship with Johnny Ramone
xref.body: Kurt Hammett of Metallica frequently visited Johnny Ramone at his Hollywood Hills home, where they bonded over a shared passion for horror movie posters. "He was often visited by Kurt Hammett of Metallica, who also had a major thing for horror movie posters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Love Triangle and Intra-Band Feud
xref.body: In 1976, Joey Ramone met 16-year-old fan Linda Danielle from Queens at CBGB. They reconnected in Los Angeles a couple of years later and became a couple, with Linda joining The Ramones on tour. Johnny Ramone, who initially made Linda sit in the back of the van, eventually discovered common ground with her (neither drank or did drugs, she liked to cook, he liked home-cooked meals) and they became best friends. Joey and Linda became engaged, but after a dispute over a ring price, Johnny realized he was in love with Linda. Johnny intimidated Joey, who hated conflict, leading Linda to move towards Johnny over the next 18 months. They broke up, and Johnny and Linda became a couple in the early 1980s, marrying in 1984. "In 1976, just as the Ramones were starting to become known, Joey met a young 16-year-old fan named Linda Danielle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mani's Music Purchase
xref.body: After deciding to form a band, D.D. Ramone and Johnny Ramone went to Mani's Music, a famous store on West 48th Street in Manhattan, where Johnny bought a guitar and D.D. acquired a bass. "They headed down to Mani's music, the famous store in West 48th Street in Manhattan, to buy some guitars and amps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Political and Personal Ideology Clash
xref.body: Joey Ramone was described as a liberal with sympathies for hippie types and progressive outlooks, while Johnny Ramone was conservative, supporting Ronald Reagan and disliking hippies. Despite these opposing views, they managed to form the band and find common ground in music. "Joey Ramon was a liberal sort of dude with sympathies for hippie types and those with progressive outlooks on life. The stars, Joey Ramon hated hippies. He was about as conservative as it got when it came to politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Romantic Entanglement and Estrangement
xref.body: Although not biological brothers, Joey and Johnny Ramone maintained a years-long estrangement. Their rift began after Johnny entered a relationship with and subsequently married Joey's girlfriend. "And although I know that they weren't really brothers, Joey and Johnny Ramone didn't talk to each other for years after Johnny stole and then married Joey's girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Stage Names and Image
xref.body: To symbolize their unity and brotherhood, all band members adopted the surname "Ramone." Jeff Hyman became Joey Ramone, Douglas Colvin became Dee Dee Ramone, John Cummings became Johnny Ramone, and Tommy kept his first name. They also adopted a uniform "tough leather jacket and jeans look." "Everybody adopted a tough leather jacket and jeans look, and everybody had a stage name. Jeff became Joey. Douglas was DD, John was Johnny, and Tommy stayed Tommy. And as a symbol of their brotherhood, they all adopted the same last name, Ramone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
